turns.reply:
Here's a wild fact to start: when you type the word "unbelievable" into an AI, it doesn't see one word.

It sees **two tokens** — roughly "un" and "believable" — each converted into a number before the model reads a single letter of your message.

That's because the first thing an LLM does is **tokenization**: it chops your text into small chunks called tokens, then maps each chunk to a number from a fixed vocabulary.

[EX]GPT-4 has a vocabulary of about 100,000 tokens. The word "bank" might be token #4,058. A space before "bank" makes it a *different* token — #8,493. Punctuation, emoji, and rare words each get their own number too.[/EX]

[KEY]Tokenization turns your words into a sequence of numbers — that's the only form an LLM can actually process.[/KEY]

Here's the thing that surprises most people: the model doesn't "read" meaning yet at this stage. It's just counting and labeling. The word "bank" (riverbank) and "bank" (financial) get the *same* token number — the model has to figure out which one you meant later.

[Q]
What does tokenization actually produce that the model works with?
A) A dictionary lookup of word definitions
B) A sequence of numbers representing text chunks
C) A compressed copy of the original sentence
ANS: B
[/Q]

turns.user: I picked B) A sequence of numbers representing text chunks
turns.reply:
That's exactly right — the model never sees letters or words, only numbers. Good.

Now here's where it gets interesting. Those numbers don't stay as a flat list for long.

Each token number gets converted into a **embedding** — a list of hundreds or thousands of decimal values that positions the token in a kind of meaning-space.

Words that tend to appear in similar contexts end up *close together* in that space. "King" and "queen" are near each other. "Bank" (financial) is near "loan" and "interest."

"Bank" (river) is near "shore" and "water."

[EX]In Google's Word2Vec embeddings (2013), researchers found you could literally do math: the vector for "king" minus "man" plus "woman" landed almost exactly on "queen." The geometry of the space captured real-world relationships.[/EX]

[KEY]An embedding turns a token number into a point in high-dimensional space, where distance encodes meaning and context.[/KEY]

This is how the model starts to handle ambiguity — the same token for "bank" gets nudged toward different neighborhoods depending on the words around it, before any prediction happens.

[Q]
Why does the embedding step matter for a word like "bank"?
A) It lets context push the token toward the right meaning before prediction
B) It compresses the token into a smaller number to save memory
C) It spells out the word so the model can read it properly
ANS: A
[/Q]

turns.user: can we keep going with the lesson
turns.reply:
You picked A — that's the right instinct, and it's the key insight: context shapes meaning *before* the model ever makes a prediction.

Now for the final piece of how this all comes together.

After tokenization and embeddings, the model runs an **attention mechanism** — it weighs how much each token should "look at" every other token in your prompt when deciding what comes next.

Then, after all that processing, the model does something surprisingly simple: it predicts the single most likely *next token*, one at a time, until the response is complete.

[EX]If you type "The cat sat on the ___", the model assigns high probability to "mat", "floor", "couch" — and near-zero probability to "democracy" or "seventeen." It picks from that probability distribution, then repeats the whole process for the token after that.[/EX]

[KEY]An LLM generates text by predicting one token at a time — always asking "given everything so far, what comes next?"[/KEY]

This is why AI can sound fluent and still be wrong: it's optimizing for *plausible next tokens*, not for *true statements*. Fluency and accuracy are different things.

Now let's put all three pieces to work.

**Your exercise:** Here's a sentence — *"After years of study, the scientist finally published her groundbreaking ___."*

Which next tokens would an LLM predict with **high confidence**? Which with **low confidence**? Pick one of each and explain *why* — using what you now know about tokenization, embeddings, and next-token prediction.

Here's something that might surprise you: when you type a message to an AI, it doesn't read your words.

Not a single one.

**Tokenization** is the first thing that happens — your text gets sliced into chunks called *tokens*, and each token gets converted to a number.

A token isn't always a word. "Unbelievable" might become two tokens: "un" and "believable." A space before a word is often its own token.

GPT-4 works with a vocabulary of roughly 100,000 possible tokens — and your entire message becomes a list of numbers before anything else happens.

[EX]The sentence "I went to the bank" becomes something like [40, 1816, 284, 262, 3331] — a sequence of integers. The model never sees letters.[/EX]

[KEY]Tokenization converts your words into numbers — that list of numbers is the only thing the model actually processes.[/KEY]

Here's why this matters: two words that *mean* the same thing might tokenize very differently, and two words that *look* similar might share tokens even when their meanings are unrelated. The model starts from numbers, not meaning.

[Q]
What does a tokenizer actually convert your text into before the model processes it?
A) A sequence of numbers representing chunks of text
B) A direct lookup in a database of facts
C) A compressed audio file of your words
ANS: A
[/Q]

Attention is the model asking: *which other tokens in this sentence should I pay attention to right now?*

[KEY]The attention mechanism lets each token "look at" every other token and update its meaning based on context — that's how the model resolves ambiguity.[/KEY]

[Q]
What problem does the attention mechanism primarily solve?
A) It speeds up how fast the model generates text
B) It checks the internet for the most relevant facts
C) It helps each token update its meaning based on surrounding context

Now for the final piece: what the model actually *does* with all that context.

After attention has done its work, the model makes one move: it predicts the **next token**.

Not the whole sentence. Not the answer. Just the single most likely next chunk of text, given everything that came before it.

Then it appends that token and does it again. And again. Your entire response is built one token at a time, each prediction feeding the next.

[EX]Given the prompt "The cat sat on the ___", the model assigns high probability to tokens like "mat," "floor," "couch" — and near-zero probability to "democracy" or "seventeen." It picks from that distribution, not from a database of correct answers.[/EX]

[KEY]An LLM generates responses by predicting one token at a time — fluency comes from pattern, not from looking anything up.[/KEY]

This is why AI can sound confident and still be completely wrong. It's optimizing for *plausible next tokens*, not for *true statements*.

[Q]
When an LLM generates a response, what is it actually doing at each step?
A) Predicting the single most likely next token given all previous tokens
B) Searching a knowledge base for the correct answer
C) Translating your question into a formal logic query
ANS: A
[/Q]

Here's something that might surprise you: the word "bank" in "I went to the bank" and "bank" in "the river bank" are treated as the **same token** — a single chunk of text with no inherent meaning attached.

That's the first puzzle an LLM has to solve before it does anything else.

It arrives as **tokens** — small chunks that might be a whole word, part of a word, or even a single punctuation mark.

---

[EX]GPT-4 uses a vocabulary of roughly 100,000 tokens. The word "unhappiness" might split into ["un", "happiness"]. The word "cat" stays as one token. A space before a word is often its own token too.[/EX]

---

The model converts each token into a number (actually a long list of numbers called a vector), and that's the only thing the math ever sees — numbers, not letters.

[KEY]Tokenization is step one: your words become numbers before the model processes anything.[/KEY]

[Q]
What is a token in an LLM?
A) A copy of a real webpage the model looks up
B) A complete sentence the model reads all at once
C) A chunk of text (word, part of a word, or punctuation) converted to a number

[/Q]
